To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
tumor uptake of macromolecules is limited by vascular extravasation and that IgG-sized constructs exhibit the optimal balance of extravasation and systemic clearance, resulting in maximal uptake.
the most effective targeting agents are macromolecules that bind with high affinity and are administered at high dose.

tumor-targeting agents with the most favorable pharmacokinetics for tumor uptake are macromolecular constructs of IgG size (150 kDa), that the dose required for saturation is inversely related to tumor antigen expression level and directly related to metabolic half-life, and that high affinity is essential for small peptides (1-10 kDa) but less important for antibodies (150 kDa) and nanoparticles (1-10 million kDa).
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a quantitative framework for the design of macromolecular agents targeted to specific tumor antigens.
the quantitative analysis of tumor-targeting agent pharmacokinetics.
the development of quantitative models that describe the pharmacokinetics of targeting agents in tumors and the use of these models for the design of improved agents.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the design of tumor targeting agents requires consideration of a wide range of factors, including agent size, affinity and target antigen, dose, and pharmacokinetic properties.
the optimal size and affinity of a targeting agent is determined by its intended application.

the optimal tumor-targeting agent should be of the size of an IgG antibody, have a high affinity for the antigen, and should be administered at the highest possible dose, consistent with toxicity considerations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a combination of small size (to enhance extravasation), high affinity (to enhance binding), and high dose (to saturate the target) is the most desirable design for tumor-targeted agents.

the design of tumor targeting agents is a complex process that requires the consideration of many factors, but the theoretical analyses presented here provide a practical framework to guide the design process.
the design of tumor targeting agents is a quantitative science, and that theoretical analyses can provide specific guidance for the design process.

the design of tumor targeting agents should be guided by quantitative models of pharmacokinetic behavior.
the design of tumor targeting agents should not rely on empirical trial-and-error, but rather be guided by a quantitative understanding of the pharmacokinetics of the agents and their targets.
